claims.text: The initial material is equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn.
Metastable solid and liquid CoCrFeNiMn states near melting can be studied at approximately 1600–2100 K.
For CoCrFeNiMn, approximately 1600–2100 K corresponds to about 0.9Tm–1.1Tm.
Static EAM references used in TOR-TILD do not adequately represent the variety of atomic configurations in the ab initio liquid.
An NN-IAP trained on representative solid and liquid AIMD configurations near melting will represent the ab initio liquid better than static EAM references.
Radial, angular, or symmetry-function descriptors can encode local many-body and subtle configurational effects in the NN-IAP.
Traditional EAM potentials miss complex many-body interactions relevant to the solid and liquid alloy.
Training on diverse AIMD configurations from both phases enables the NN-IAP to learn interactions missing from EAM.
Learning these interactions will produce a closer approximation to the ab initio energy landscape.
A closer approximation to the ab initio energy landscape will improve reference–target phase-space overlap.
Improved reference–target phase-space overlap will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch.
The NN-IAP will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by approximately 40–50% relative to TOR-TILD EAM references.
NN-IAP-based free-energy differences will converge to within approximately 10 meV/atom of full ab initio benchmarks.
The intervention is expected to be most effective for alloys similar to equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn between 0.9Tm and 1.1Tm.
Use outside the specified composition or temperature regime may require additional training data or methodological adjustments.
Insufficient representation of rare high-energy configurations or transition states may cause NN-IAP extrapolation errors.
Such extrapolation errors could make the reduction in thermodynamic-integration mismatch smaller than predicted.
The comparison should use parallel NN-IAP and EAM-based thermodynamic-integration simulations under identical conditions and integration pathways.
Failure to reduce mismatch by at least approximately 40%, or failure to converge within approximately 10 meV/atom of an ab initio benchmark, is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.
